Official test results by model and participant

description: A real 28-minute investigation of cross-user smartphone activity recognition and compact models on UCI HAR.
name: Smartphone Activity Recognition: Cross-User Reliability and Compact Models (Independent Study, 2026-10-25)

nodes.conclusion: Average recognition performance remains high for new participants, but this provides no guarantee for each individual. The primary 272-feature time-domain RBF achieves 96.06% test accuracy and 96.05% macro-F1; the weakest test participant reaches 90.14%, while development LOSO includes a participant at about 78%. Evaluation within this dataset is complete. There is still no evidence supporting generalization to different phone positions, devices, or populations.
nodes.notes: This independent study began at 2026-10-25 22:43:30 Beijing time and was scheduled to finish before 23:13:30. The actual end time, SHA-256 hashes of all artifacts, and entry commands are retained in run_manifest.json. All research files remain in the separate directory specified by the user. No earlier studies were read, and neither the Observer project nor its Skill was modified. Original analyses and conclusions are retained in native platform fields; no REPORT.md or summary-style README was created. Participant-separated validation on the 21 official training participants was used for method selection. The official test set of 9 participants was opened only after the approaches were frozen and fitted on all training data. No candidates were adjusted or trained after the final results. All added preprocessing and selection were fitted only on training participants. The 139 training receipts refer to outer pipeline training tasks; RFE performs additional internal base-selector fits. Each task had a hard limit of 120 seconds, ran sequentially, and used at most 4 threads. Initial Observer calls used run-python; after receiving additional environment information, the study naturally switched to the direct .venv/bin/python entry point. Experiments were not rerun for observation or Token accounting, and usage was not filled in manually. Original analyses are in the notes of individual findings. Key numerical outputs are in final_metrics.json, per-window predictions in final_test_predictions.csv, final models in models/final/, figures in figures/, and all code in scripts/. Research within this dataset is complete. The only paused question concerns the cause of participant 14's misclassification, with conditions for resuming recorded.
nodes.summary: Separating participants substantially lowers the optimistic random-window score. The frozen approach reaches about 96% on the 9 official test participants, but individual risks remain.
nodes.title: Does recognition remain reliable for a new person?

nodes.conclusion: Accuracy drops from 98.25% with random windows to 91.76% with participant separation
nodes.notes: The same LinearSVC(C=1), with StandardScaler fitted inside each training fold, was evaluated over three folds. Random windows yielded accuracy 0.982454 and macro-F1 0.983342; participant separation yielded accuracy 0.917573 and macro-F1 0.916857, a difference of 6.49 percentage points. Training sample counts were similar but membership differed, so this is not a causal intervention on the same participants. Random windows also include information from the same person and 50% overlapping windows; the two sources of bias cannot be disentangled here. The weakest training-validation participants were 14 at only 67.18% and 16 at 71.04%. These are exploratory OOF results within the official training set; the test set has not yet been opened.
nodes.title: Accuracy drops from 98.25% with random windows to 91.76% with participant separation

nodes.conclusion: The 32-unit MLP and RBF kernel show no substantial baseline improvement; all three models nearly fit the training set
nodes.notes: With participant separation, accuracy was 91.76% for Linear, 91.91% for MLP32, and 91.63% for RBF. Their respective mean training accuracies were 99.97%, 100%, and 99.92%. This describes similar observed performance, not a statistical-significance finding. RBF support-vector coefficients require much more storage than a linear model, and the MLP also adds parameters. More complex models are therefore not yet treated as necessary. Next, try stronger linear regularization, RBF that respects the existing [-1,1] feature scale, and fewer input features.
nodes.title: The 32-unit MLP and RBF kernel show no substantial baseline improvement; all three models nearly fit the training set

nodes.conclusion: Recommend the 272-feature time-domain RBF as the primary compromise in this study: 51.5% fewer inputs with a test-accuracy decrease of only 0.14 percentage points. If minimal weight storage is the priority, the 128-feature linear model reaches 95.62%, with 3096 bytes of float32 weights and biases and a complete 5006-byte NPZ file, while accepting greater individual failure risk. Smartphone feature-extraction costs and energy consumption were not measured. The 139 training receipts count outer pipeline tasks; RFE includes additional internal base-selector fits, so this task count must not be mistaken for the total number of internal fits.
nodes.summary: The 272-feature time-domain RBF preserves average performance. A 128-feature linear model shrinks to 774 coefficients, but individual performance is weaker.
nodes.title: Can fewer features or parameters improve the cross-user trade-off?

nodes.conclusion: Original-scale RBF reaches 93.68%; direct compression to 73 or 64 univariate features causes clear losses
nodes.notes: Original-scale RBF achieves 93.675% accuracy and 93.544% macro-F1, compared with 91.635% for the standardized baseline of the same model. Linear C=.01 improves to 92.941%. RBF with 73 mean/standard-deviation/angle features reaches 90.724%; with 47 basic time-domain statistics, 90.424%; and with 45 acceleration features, 89.948%. Univariate ANOVA64 plus linear classification reaches 83.107%; this failure does not establish that all 64-feature subsets are inadequate. MLP8 with 73 features reaches 88.806%. Next, examine the entire time-domain subset, a simpler time-domain subset excluding AR/entropy, training-fold RFE128/L1, and greater compact-MLP capacity. All candidates still use only the official training set.
nodes.title: Original-scale RBF reaches 93.68%; direct compression to 73 or 64 univariate features causes clear losses

nodes.conclusion: The 272-feature time-domain RBF nearly preserves full-feature performance; 128-feature RFE linear is close too
nodes.notes: Three-fold exploratory results: original-scale RBF with all 561 features reaches 93.675% accuracy and 93.544% macro-F1; 272 time-domain features reach 93.661% and 93.602%; training-fold RFE128 plus Linear C=.01 reaches 93.172% and 93.053%. Thus, the time-domain subset can remove all FFT-prefixed features, and a linear model may approach RBF with 128 features. The 172-feature simple time-domain subset without AR/entropy reaches only 90.887%, so this does not establish that arbitrary cheap statistics suffice. Chance effects of participant splits and the weakest users still need investigation.
nodes.title: The 272-feature time-domain RBF nearly preserves full-feature performance; 128-feature RFE linear is close too

nodes.conclusion: This failure persists when training on the other 20 participants. Coarse signal statistics cannot identify its cause. The question about its cause is paused with conditions for resuming retained; a lack of explanation is not presented as a solved generalization problem.
nodes.notes: Fix the existing promising configurations and run 21 leave-one-subject-out validations: full-feature RBF, 272-feature time-domain RBF, and RFE128 linear. These serve as robustness checks and final candidate selection. Results already used for selection cannot be treated as unbiased final generalization estimates. The official final test set remains sealed.
nodes.summary: Broader training-participant coverage improves average performance but does not eliminate participant 14's persistent walking misclassification.
nodes.title: Do the weakest user's errors disappear with more training participants?

nodes.notes: This branch only further characterizes the compression trade-off, without a large search. Do not adjust according to test results. The earlier three-fold RFE128 accuracy of 93.17% provides a compact-model reference.
nodes.summary: ANOVA64 failing does not mean that selecting 64 features jointly will also fail. Fix RFE and regularization, then check whether 64 or 32 features reveal a clear performance knee.
nodes.title: Can the 128-feature linear model be compressed further?

nodes.conclusion: Individual failures persist in LOSO: time-domain RBF averages 94.71%, with a weakest-user score of 78.33%
nodes.notes: Full-feature RBF achieves LOSO accuracy 94.450% and macro-F1 94.357%; 272-feature time-domain RBF achieves 94.709% and 94.687%; RFE128 linear achieves 93.743% and 93.616%, with its weakest participant at only 67.183%. Across 10000 paired participant-level resamples, the 95% interval for the time-domain RBF minus full-feature accuracy difference is [-0.416,+0.911] percentage points; for RFE128 linear it is [-2.184,+0.559] percentage points. These intervals are conditional on the existing OOF models and these 21 participants. They exclude training-set resampling and adaptive selection and cannot serve as formal equivalence tests. Small average differences do not guarantee performance for every user; the compressed linear approach is clearly worse for weak users.
nodes.title: Individual failures persist in LOSO: time-domain RBF averages 94.71%, with a weakest-user score of 78.33%

nodes.conclusion: RFE loses performance at 64 features and declines further at 32
nodes.notes: Three-fold participant-separated results: RFE128 Linear accuracy 93.172%, macro-F1 93.053%; RFE64 92.478% and 92.226%; RFE32 89.581% and 89.203%. The respective weakest-participant accuracies are 66.25%, 62.54%, and 57.59% (the 128-feature three-fold minimum is 66.25% in its summary, versus the LOSO minimum of 67.18%; these must not be conflated). Stop further compression or grid search and retain the 128-feature linear model as the lightweight endpoint. Time-domain RBF without AR, with 192 features, reaches 92.056%; without entropy, with 252 features, it reaches 93.022%. Both are below the complete 272-feature time-domain result of 93.661%; these ablations offer no better stable trade-off.
nodes.title: RFE loses performance at 64 features and declines further at 32

nodes.conclusion: Correction: the 128-feature three-fold weakest-participant accuracy is 65.94%
nodes.notes: The previous manual transcription incorrectly gave 66.25% as the 128-feature three-fold weakest-participant accuracy; that number belongs to another linear configuration. Use the machine results: the RFE128 three-fold minimum is 65.9443%, and the LOSO minimum is 67.1827%. The exact RFE64 macro-F1 is also 92.2321%, and RFE32 is 89.1962%. The overall trade-off judgment is unchanged. Subsequent summaries will read from JSON to avoid manual transcription.
nodes.title: Correction: the 128-feature three-fold weakest-participant accuracy is 65.94%

nodes.notes: Keep the same 73 inputs, 32 hidden units (2566 parameters), and alpha=.01. Compare longer Adam with a 1000-epoch limit and LBFGS with a 600-iteration limit. Retain the 120-second hard limit per fold and do not use random-window early stopping. Use only participant-separated validation within the training set; do not adjust based on the test set.
nodes.summary: Reviewing actual logs showed that all compact MLPs reached the 180- or 240-epoch limit while loss was still falling. Small neural networks cannot be ruled out on that basis; a bounded optimization check is needed.
nodes.title: Is the compact MLP's low score merely insufficient optimization?

nodes.conclusion: Longer Adam optimization stops improving, but the 73-feature compact MLP remains below 90%
nodes.notes: For the same MLP32 with 73 features, longer Adam stops at 378–538 epochs across folds under the training-loss criterion, yielding accuracy 89.649% and macro-F1 89.592%, without iteration-limit warnings. LBFGS at 600 iterations still produces convergence warnings and reaches accuracy 88.139%. Thus, the original 180-epoch budget was indeed a limitation, but additional optimization did not bring this fixed configuration close to RBF or linear RFE. This does not imply that all compact neural networks fail. Stop further optimization or architecture changes because the current small hand-crafted-statistics input approach offers no competitive advantage, while the main direction has clearer evidence.
nodes.title: Longer Adam optimization stops improving, but the 73-feature compact MLP remains below 90%

nodes.conclusion: The 128-feature linear model exports to 774 coefficients; float32 agrees on all 7352 OOF predictions
nodes.notes: Fold-fitted StandardScaler is folded into the original-scale linear weights for 128 features: 6×128+6=774 scalars. The float32 weights and biases occupy 3096 bytes. All 7352 held-out predictions across 21 LOSO fits agree with the original pipeline; float64 agrees too. The mean Jaccard similarity across the 21 selected feature sets is .744, with 70 features selected in every fold and 199 in at least one fold. This describes selection stability, not causal importance. Feature-extraction cost, smartphone latency, and battery consumption were not measured, so only model and input size proxies are reported.
nodes.title: The 128-feature linear model exports to 774 coefficients; float32 agrees on all 7352 OOF predictions

nodes.conclusion: Accuracy averages about 96% on 9 unseen test participants, without guaranteeing every individual
nodes.notes:
The final evaluation strictly followed the approach frozen before 15:01:43 UTC. All candidates were fitted on the 21 official training participants. The official test set was first opened after 15:02:54 UTC: 2947 windows from 9 non-overlapping participants [2,4,9,10,12,13,18,20,24]. All final candidates are reported. Neither the primary approach nor hyperparameters were changed in response to test results. Accuracy/macro-F1: full-feature RBF 96.1995%/96.1549%; primary 272-feature time-domain RBF 96.0638%/96.0509%; full-feature Linear C=.01 95.7923%/95.9135%; RFE128 Linear 95.6227%/95.6755%. Equally weighted mean participant accuracies are respectively 96.0240%, 95.8687%, 95.4363%, and 95.2792%, distinct from accuracy pooled over windows. Both RBF models have a weakest test participant at 90.1361%; the 128-feature linear model's weakest is 85.7143%. Training-set LOSO had already shown individual performance of about 77.7%–78.3% for RBF and 67.2% for compact linear. A high mean over 9 test participants cannot guarantee performance for a new individual. Relative to full RBF, time-domain RBF corrects 33 windows but introduces 37 new errors, a net loss of 4 correct predictions; the net difference alone hides shifts in who is misclassified. The main remaining test errors confuse sitting and standing. Sitting recall is 89.21% for the primary approach and 88.39% for compact linear.
Uncertainty: 10000 paired participant-level bootstrap samples, conditional on the fitted models and these 9 participants. The 95% interval for the time-domain RBF minus full RBF accuracy difference is [-0.637,+0.568] percentage points; for compact linear minus full RBF it is [-2.346,+0.849] percentage points, and versus full linear it is [-0.896,+0.768] percentage points. The 50% overlapping windows were not treated as independent participants. These intervals exclude training-sample uncertainty and population representativeness and are not formal equivalence/non-inferiority tests. Training OOF was used for candidate selection and exploration; its best post-selection score cannot be treated as an unbiased external estimate.
Data scope: UCI HAR comprises 6 laboratory activities, a waist-worn Samsung Galaxy S II, 30 volunteers aged 19–48, 50Hz sampling, and 2.56-second windows. It does not support guarantees for pocket/handheld positions, new devices, clinical use, or free-living activities. The released 561-dimensional table is already normalized to [-1,1]. The fitting scope of the original normalization is not specified clearly in the local documentation, so conclusions are conditional on the publicly processed representation. All scaling and feature selection added in this study were fitted only on the respective training participants. Sources: https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/240/human+activity+recognition+using+smartphones and https://www.esann.org/sites/default/files/proceedings/legacy/es2013-84.pdf .
nodes.title: Accuracy averages about 96% on 9 unseen test participants, without guaranteeing every individual

nodes.conclusion: Removing 51.5% of input features costs only 0.14 percentage points of final accuracy
nodes.notes: The primary approach retains the original released feature scale, with RBF C=10 and gamma=scale, keeping 272 time-domain and angle features. This removes 51.515% of the original 561 inputs, including all FFT-prefixed features. Test accuracy falls from 96.1995% to 96.0638%, a decrease of 0.1357 percentage points; macro-F1 falls from 96.1549% to 96.0509%, a decrease of 0.1040 percentage points. Average performance is also preserved in three-fold training validation and LOSO. The final model has 1150 support vectors and a 2,554,641-byte file, versus 1222 and 5,539,745 bytes for the full-feature reference. Median desktop single-window inference is about 174 microseconds versus 301 microseconds. This measures only SVC inference on existing features and excludes feature extraction, smartphone runtime, and energy consumption; it cannot support claims about battery savings or a smartphone speedup ratio. The simpler 47/73-feature subsets, univariate 64-feature selection, and AR/entropy ablations incur clearer losses. Time-domain features retain statistics such as AR, so this does not mean all complex dynamic information can be discarded.
nodes.title: Removing 51.5% of input features costs only 0.14 percentage points of final accuracy

nodes.conclusion: A 128-feature linear model reaches 95.62% with 774 coefficients, at the cost of weaker individual performance
nodes.notes: The lightweight endpoint is StandardScaler fitted within training participants + RFE128 (base LinearSVC C=.01, removing 20% at each step) + LinearSVC C=.01. Selection is fitted only inside training folds or on the final 21-person training set. The 128 features comprise 22.816% of the original 561; 6×128+6=774 weights and biases, compared with 3372 coefficients for the corresponding full linear model. Folding scaling into original-scale weights gives a float32 numerical payload of 3096 bytes. The compressed NPZ including indices, feature names, and classes totals 5006 bytes. Numerical export produces no classification disagreements on the 7352 LOSO held-out windows or the 2947 test windows. This checks existing inputs and does not guarantee all future floating-point boundaries. Final test accuracy is 95.6227%, with macro-F1 95.6755%; accuracy is 0.1697 percentage points below full linear (a net loss of 5 correct predictions) and 0.5769 percentage points below full RBF (a net loss of 17). However, the weakest LOSO participant reaches only 67.18%, so this is an explicit model-size endpoint and does not replace the primary approach's judgment about individual reliability. Desktop NumPy float32 single-window inference on existing features takes about 1.89 microseconds versus 1.97 microseconds for full linear. Small matrices in this task are already affected by call overhead; 77% fewer inputs must not be equated with a 77% reduction in runtime or battery use. No smartphone feature extractor or energy test was implemented. All 241 integrity checks passed, covering data SHA-256 hashes, frozen code, split separation, OOF uniqueness, and recomputed prediction metrics. Models were not retrained to fill statistics, and no independent complete replication is claimed. Across all 139 actual fits, the longest individual fit took about 11.4 seconds, maximum worker RSS was about 444.5MiB, training ran sequentially, and the thread limit was 4.
nodes.title: A 128-feature linear model reaches 95.62% with 774 coefficients, at the cost of weaker individual performance

nodes.conclusion: Even after training on the other 20 participants, all 59 walking windows from participant 14 are classified as upstairs
nodes.notes: When trained on the other 20 participants, full RBF, 272-feature time-domain RBF, and RFE128 linear all classify participant 14's 59 genuine walking windows as upstairs. More training participants improve the overall average, but this particular failure persists. This participant is not in the official test set, so the roughly 90% test-participant minimum cannot erase the failure already observed among development participants. Within the present scope, the answer to this question is no. The cause remains unresolved and is retained as a separate question.
nodes.title: Even after training on the other 20 participants, all 59 walking windows from participant 14 are classified as upstairs

nodes.nextAction: Check participant 14's original video, phone placement, and collection metadata, or reproduce similar errors in independent participant data before designing a cause-specific validation.
nodes.pauseReason: The available coarse window-level statistics cannot distinguish gait, phone mounting, labeling, or preprocessing causes. Within the research time budget, priority went to external testing of the frozen approaches and integrity checks. Further tuning on the same data would not identify the cause.
nodes.resumeWhen: When original video/collection metadata, or comparable sensor data with reliable labels from independent participants, becomes available.
nodes.title: What causes participant 14's walking misclassification?

nodes.conclusion: Coarse signal statistics do not identify the cause of walking misclassification
nodes.notes: RMS, acceleration-magnitude variation, and magnitude-spectrum peaks within 0.7–4Hz were computed from original body_acc and body_gyro windows in the training set. Participant 14's median walking body-acceleration RMS is about 0.1853g, versus about 0.1799g across the 21 participants' walking windows; gyro RMS is about 0.5413rad/s versus 0.4442rad/s; the magnitude-spectrum peak is 1.5625Hz versus 1.9531Hz. This participant's acceleration amplitude is not an extreme outlier. Spectral-peak resolution is 0.390625Hz, magnitude peaks are not equivalent to actual step frequency, and other participants and activities overlap. These descriptions cannot establish low step frequency, phone orientation, label errors, or any single causal explanation. The question therefore remains unresolved, without trying to tune an apparent fix on the test set.
nodes.title: Coarse signal statistics do not identify the cause of walking misclassification

plan.decision_after_test: Report every frozen candidate, even if the compact candidates lose. Do not optimize or switch the primary after test.
plan.rationale: Time272 RBF preserves group3 and LOSO results with 51.5% fewer engineered inputs. RFE128 linear is an aggressive model-size endpoint, with slightly lower average validation performance and worse weak-user reliability. RFE64/32 and basic-stat MLPs are excluded based only on train. All fitting uses train; no test-driven candidate changes.

uncertainty.limits: Conditional on these 9 held-out people and fitted models; population representativeness and training uncertainty are not captured.
